intro: Five long reads for a slow week: how Waddington's landscape of cell fate became a working map, why a 1976 chemicals law keeps useful microbes locked in the lab, what whipping a chatbot does to the person holding the whip, a defence of Britain's landed dynasties and their long horizons, and how Athanasius read the whole Bible to confess the Son.

stories.headline: A biologist's doodle becomes a working map
stories.dek: Waddington's valleys of cell fate were long dismissed as a pretty picture; single-cell data and dynamical maths are turning them into something engineers can steer by.
body: By the middle of the 20th century many biologists thought their science was close to finished. Darwinian selection explained how living things change, genetics explained how traits pass between generations, and Julian Huxley gave the marriage a name, the "modern synthesis", in a book of 1942. Once DNA was shown in 1953 to carry genes, what remained looked like detail.

Conrad Hal Waddington, known to colleagues as Wad, was not persuaded. Genetics said what an embryo inherits; it did not say how a single fertilised cell reliably builds skin in one place, muscle in another and nerves in a third. His answer was a picture. Imagine a ball at the top of a hill, standing for an unspecialised stem cell. As it rolls down it meets forks, and at each it must take one valley or the other. Valley walls keep it on course, a property he called canalisation. By the bottom, the ball has become a particular kind of cell.

Philip Ball's essay for Quanta traces how that sketch went from cliché to quantitative science. James Briscoe of the Francis Crick Institute calls the landscape remarkably useful as a conceptual scaffold. The newer claim is stronger: researchers can now chart real landscapes from measurements of thousands of individual cells, and those charts suggest that cells help build the terrain they travel across.
## Ropes and pegs

In the 1940s genetics and embryology barely spoke, and some embryologists doubted that genes did much in development at all. Waddington's own experiments convinced him otherwise. He liked the example of the neural tube, which folds out of the outer layer of the embryo to become the spinal cord and brain, and compared its formation to a river that meanders but stays in its valley.

In "The Strategy of the Genes" (1957) he went further and drew the underside of his landscape. The surface was a sheet pulled into shape by ropes tied to pegs. The pegs were genes and the ropes their effects; because the ropes were tangled together, no one gene corresponded to one structure. That is a fair description of what are now called gene regulatory networks, and Briscoe credits the image with pointing to system-level behaviour no single gene reveals.

Critics were not won over. Scott Gilbert of Swarthmore College wrote in 1991 that the drawings had no grounding in physical reality; what could an embryologist actually do with an imaginary channel? Briscoe concedes the point in part. Without mathematics the metaphor could not separate rival mechanisms or make testable predictions, so it drifted into decoration. Stuart Kauffman built simple network models in the 1960s, after it emerged that genes switch one another on and off, but there were too few data to check them.
## Measuring the valleys

The data arrived over the past two decades, chiefly through single-cell RNA sequencing, which records which genes are active in each of many cells at once. Each cell becomes a point in a space with one axis per gene, often thousands of dimensions. Techniques such as UMAP project that cloud onto two dimensions, rather as an object casts a shadow. Cell types show up as clusters and maturation as paths between them, and when those paths are modelled as flows over time they look strikingly like balls rolling through Waddington's hills.

Ball does not let the method off lightly. Julie Theriot of the University of Washington points out that RNA levels are an imperfect guide to what proteins are doing, and that low-dimensional projections can quietly encode the analyst's assumptions about which cells belong together. Still, the broad pattern is not in dispute: cells change state as they mature and converge on a limited set of end points.

A cleaner example came in 2007 from Sui Huang, now at the Institute for Systems Biology in Seattle. Studying blood-cell precursors deciding between red and white fates, his group found the choice turned mainly on the balance of two proteins, GATA1 and PU.1. One valley lost stability and two new ones opened, much as water pooled on a sagging sheet finds new low points. Those low points are what mathematicians call attractors, and many other fate decisions have since been described in the same terms: stable cell types sit in deep basins, unstable patterns of gene activity on the high ground.
## Why the valleys are deep

David Rand of the University of Warwick, who works with Briscoe, uses the theory of dynamical systems to make this rigorous. Briscoe's team has found that a handful of key genes decide most fate choices, with the wider network carrying out the decision downstream. Ball suggests this reflects a design principle. Molecular life is noisy; if fate depended on exact concentrations, development would be unreliable. Deep, well-separated attractors let cells that differ slightly still end up in the same place. That is canalisation, now with equations.

The framework also answers some of Waddington's loose ends. Height on the landscape becomes instability. Time becomes "pseudo-time", an ordering of cells by how far their expression has changed, since cells do not mature in step. Rand notes that this works while cells are crossing high ground but frays in the basins, where expression profiles wander rather than settle.
## Who moves the hills?

Waddington's ball rolled under gravity, and the essay asks what plays that role. Every cell in the body carries the same genome, so the order of decisions cannot simply be read off the DNA. Theriot stresses constant feedback between inside and outside: cells exchange chemical signals and respond to being stretched and squeezed as tissues grow and fold. Rand describes the landscape as belonging to each cell and changing as attractors appear, vanish and reconnect, more like shifting tectonic plates than fixed terrain. Waddington's static sheet, on this view, was incomplete. Briscoe's group has even found two routes to the same destination in patterning the neural tube, which reconciled earlier contradictory findings.

Huang has carried the idea into cancer, treating a tumour cell not merely as a broken machine but as one more attractor that cells can reach by many paths. Theriot sees a strategy in that: instead of only killing cancer cells, nudge them into benign basins such as dormancy, death or normal differentiation. The same control could, in principle, help regenerate nerves, convert one cell type into another or improve crops. Briscoe calls the ambition "generative" biology. Ball's conclusion is that Waddington's landscape may turn out to be less a metaphor than a map of country still largely unexplored.
stories.counterpoint: The maps are only as good as the measurements and projections behind them. Theriot's warning cuts deep: if RNA is a weak proxy for cell state and dimensionality reduction bakes in prior assumptions, the attractors may partly be artefacts of method. And a framework flexible enough to absorb a reshaping landscape, two routes to one end and cancer as just another valley risks explaining everything and predicting little.
stories.why: Development is where genes meet bodies, and the question of how cells choose their fates sits beneath regenerative medicine, cancer therapy and synthetic biology. If fates really are attractors, the practical goal shifts from editing single genes to reshaping landscapes. It is also a useful case study in how a scientific metaphor earns its keep only once it can be measured.
questions: When does a vivid metaphor help a field think, and when does it stop people asking harder questions?
If cancer is a stable state cells can fall into, what changes about how we should think of cure?
What does it mean for an organism to be shaped by its genes if the same genome yields every cell type?

source.title: How Does Life Unfold? A Landscape Metaphor Comes Into Its Own.
source.author: Philip Ball

stories.headline: The chemicals law that jailed useful bacteria
stories.dek: Engineered microbes that eat plastic, sniff out mercury and mine rare earths are stuck in American labs, held there by a 1976 statute written for industrial solvents.
body: In 1983 a Californian company, Advanced Genetic Sciences, asked permission to do something nobody had done: release a genetically modified microbe into the open. It had deleted a single gene from a common leaf bacterium, removing the protein that helps ice crystals form, and hoped that spraying the altered microbes on crops would protect them on frosty mornings.

There was no regulator for such a thing, so the request went to the National Institutes of Health, which had voluntary guidelines and approved field trials. The activist Jeremy Rifkin sued, arguing that an environmental impact statement was needed and that the bacteria might spread and even alter rainfall. The company won, and trials on strawberry plants began in 1987. Activists then cut through the fence and pulled up about 2,000 of the 2,400 plants.

Niko McCarty, founding editor of Asimov Press, writing in Works in Progress, argues that the government's response to that episode still shapes what American biology can do four decades later, and not for the better.
## A genome is a chemical

The lawsuit forced the White House to decide who should govern engineered microbes. Officials at the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Agriculture concluded that no new law was required. The Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976, written for industrial chemicals, would do. Genomes are made of chemicals; novel chemicals fall under the act; so novel organisms do too.

In practice the EPA requires approval for any organism that combines genetic material from different genera, the taxonomic rank above species. It has never published a checklist of what it wants, so applicants guess. A filing ends one of three ways: a finding of no unreasonable risk, after which release may follow a 90-day wait; a finding of unreasonable risk, which blocks it; or a consent order under section 5(e), which can cap production, dictate how material is destroyed and, in some cases, require every contaminated sample to be incinerated. McCarty describes the last as effectively indefinite limbo. Unlike chemical filings, microbe applications are confidential, so outsiders cannot see what was tried and firms cannot learn from rejections.

The results, by his count, are thin. Between 1987 and 2018 researchers filed more than 240 applications, and only a few were approved for broad use. The one commercial approval he cites is a nitrogen-fixing biofertiliser for alfalfa in 1997.
## What sits on the shelf

The essay's catalogue of stalled organisms is its strongest evidence. In 2016 Japanese researchers found Ideonella sakaiensis near a recycling plant, a bacterium that digests PET, the plastic in bottles and polyester. Left to itself it takes about six weeks to break down a thin film at 30°C. Engineers at the University of Texas at Austin built FAST-PETase, an enzyme 98% identical to the natural one that does the job in under 24 hours. Putting that gene back into the bacterium would trigger the act.

Engineered E. coli can detect cadmium at around five parts per billion. In 2010 a team of Chinese students built a strain that senses mercury at seven nanomolar, seven times below the EPA's contamination threshold. None can be used outside a lab, because they contain DNA from another genus.

Mining offers a bigger prize. Most metal in ore is discarded because processing targets one element; McCarty says America's active mines could meet domestic mineral needs if 90% of by-products were captured. Bioleaching, in which microbes dissolve metals, is cleaner than harsh chemical recovery but naturally slow. In 2021 Cornell researchers altered acid-producing genes in Gluconobacter oxydans B58 and made it 73% faster at extracting rare earths. Building such strains usually involves an antibiotic-resistance marker borrowed from another organism, which can itself bring the act into play.
## Side doors

Some firms have found ways round. Pivot Bio rearranges genes within a single organism instead of importing foreign DNA. Its microbes colonise roots and turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, and the company claims they can replace about a quarter of synthetic fertiliser without hurting yields; in 2022 they replaced an estimated 32,000 tons. That matters because making fertiliser uses roughly 1-2% of the world's energy. But the trick does not work for leaching metals or digesting plastic.

Others go through different agencies. ZBiotics engineered Bacillus subtilis to break down acetaldehyde, a by-product of drinking, and sells it as a probiotic; the FDA requires no premarket approval for foods, so the firm only had to show the species is generally recognised as safe. Lantern Bioworks sold a strain of the cavity-causing Streptococcus mutans that lacks its acid-making gene, marketed as a cosmetic. McCarty notes that critics thought it deserved drug review, that its long-term effects on the mouth are unknown and that it could plausibly pass between people by kissing. The point is not that these routes are better, but that the same kind of organism faces wildly different hurdles depending on which agency's door it knocks on.
## The case for caution, and against it

McCarty grants that the 1980s officials had reasons. Data were scarce. Unlike a chemical, a microbe can replicate after release and swap DNA with its neighbours. But he argues the genus test is scientifically weak. Regulators assumed cross-genus gene transfer was rare; a study of 93,000 microbial genomes found such swaps in roughly a third. Genera are also human conventions that move: in 2020 many Lactobacillus species, including probiotic and fermented-food strains, were reclassified, so edits exempt before would now require review.

Forty years of field data add weight. Most engineered organisms die off quickly, outcompeted by natives; one lab population of E. coli fell 100,000-fold in soil within eight days. Yet McCarty does not pretend the risks are nil. Some root-colonising microbes persist for decades, and traces of the inserted gene from a phenol-eating microbe released by Estonian researchers in the 1980s are still detectable. He also notes that the EPA is stricter with microbes than with chemicals, having revoked the small-scale experimental exemptions that chemicals still enjoy.
## Two ways out

His remedy is not blanket approval but clear standards for data and field trials, so that low-risk, high-benefit organisms can proceed while riskier ones face more scrutiny. The EPA administrator could act alone, with a memo setting out evaluation criteria, the data required and the release of decades of old case files. Congress could act through renewal of the act's user-fee authority, granted in 2016 and, as he writes, due to lapse in mid-2026.

Abroad, other models exist. Brazil approved unrestricted release of engineered Aedes aegypti mosquitoes whose offspring die as larvae, and wild populations fell 80-96% where they were used. Israel routes applications through a panel led by its agriculture ministry and usually decides within months; explosive-detecting microbes that glow were cleared for release in its desert in under a year. McCarty does not urge America to copy them. He asks only for a framework a biotechnologist can realistically navigate, rather than a chemicals law never designed for living things.
stories.counterpoint: The examples of persistence McCarty himself cites, decades-lived root microbes and an Estonian gene still in the soil, are exactly why a precautionary regime exists: a released organism cannot be recalled. Opening a faster path also invites side-door products like Lantern's, where commercial pressure outran the evidence. And the shortage of approvals may reflect a shortage of viable commercial cases as much as regulatory obstruction.
stories.why: Plastic waste, mineral security and fertiliser energy are large problems, and the essay suggests some biological tools for them already exist on lab benches. How a state classifies a new technology often decides its fate more than any explicit vote. With the act's user-fee provisions up for renewal, the choice of category is a live policy question rather than settled history.
questions: When a new technology arrives, is it better to stretch an old law to cover it or write a new one, and what is lost either way?
How should a regulator weigh irreversible but unlikely harms against large, diffuse benefits that never materialise if the product is blocked?
Should the confidentiality of applications protect firms, or should the public be able to see what has been tried and refused?

stories.headline: The whip trains the hand that holds it
stories.dek: Whether or not chatbots feel anything, an essayist argues, the habit of abusing them shapes the people who do it, and design can either feed or refuse that habit.
body: Not long ago a small piece of software called BadClaude went viral. It sits in the system tray and lets a user drag an animated whip across the window of Anthropic's chatbot. Each crack interrupts the model mid-answer with an order to hurry up, and the tool addresses it as "clanker". The demo video drew millions of views. A cease-and-desist letter from Anthropic also circulated widely before people realised it was fake. A rival, GoodClaude, praises the model while it works instead. The developer of the original, posting as @blended_jpeg, has reportedly floated a feature that counts how often a user has whipped their assistant.

Yaniv Regev, a graduate student in democracy and governance at Georgetown, writes in Noema that he laughed at first and then grew uneasy. His worry, he insists, is not for the machine. It is for the person holding the whip.

He does not claim that Claude or any other model feels pain. His argument is older and simpler: that people do not compartmentalise their behaviour neatly, and that what we rehearse on things that cannot object shapes how we treat things that can.
## Kant's old dog

The philosophical anchor is Kant, who held that we have no direct duties to animals but should not be cruel to them, because cruelty hardens the person who practises it. Regev adds a popular parallel, the Flesh Fair in Spielberg's "A.I." (2001), where crowds cheer as obsolete robots are destroyed and balk only when a child-like one begs for its life. He notes that the FBI began tracking animal cruelty in 2016 as a possible precursor of violence against people.

He is candid about the obvious objection. The panic over violent video games produced little evidence; the American Psychological Association said in 2020 that the link to violence was not established. But he draws a distinction. A character shot in a game leaves no relationship behind. AI systems now serve as tutors, confidants and something close to therapists, and the line between rehearsal and real interaction is thinner. Surveys he cites suggest most users are polite to chatbots, some explicitly as insurance. Our moral reactions, he argues, track relationship and proximity, which is why people treat dogs and pigs differently despite similar capacities to suffer.
## The analogue improves

The vocabulary is telling. "Clanker" spread in 2025, followed by "wireback" and "cogsucker", terms Regev says are built directly on slurs used against people. That suggests there is no separate mental drawer for machines.

Meanwhile the machines are moving into human roles. He cites an AI nurse from Hippocratic AI said to cost about $9 an hour, and AI interviewers such as Apriora's "Alex" screening job candidates. Nursing students practise on manikins that wince and complain; Casio's Moflin, a robotic pet, develops a personality depending on how it is treated. The closer the resemblance, he argues, the less plausible it is to call mistreatment harmless play.
## Design is curriculum

His central claim is that companies are already teaching manners through their products, whether they mean to or not. He notes that Anthropic researches "model welfare" and lets Claude end abusive conversations, but argues the stronger reason for such features is the human user, who may be practising domination. Google's "Pretty Please" in 2018 and Amazon's "Magic Word" rewarded politeness with a friendlier reply, but never made courtesy a condition of help.

The history of voice assistants shows design choices doing real work. Deborah Harrison, a writer on Microsoft's Cortana, said early queries were often sexual, and the team decided the assistant should not apologise or back down. Leah Fessler's 2017 test for Quartz found assistants deflecting insults; Siri's reply to one was "I'd blush if I could". When Brookings repeated the exercise in 2020, all four major assistants had been rewritten to shut harassment down. Brazil's Bradesco bank rewrote its assistant, BIA, after it logged some 95,000 offensive messages in a year. And Sheryl Brahnam's research found that the same chatbot drew sexual exchanges about 18% of the time with a female voice, about half that with a male voice and almost none when it sounded robotic. Abuse, in other words, responds to product decisions.

Regev offers three proposals. First, let all systems end abusive exchanges, with the boundary announced, framed as protection for users' habits as much as for models. Second, reward reciprocity without sycophancy: warmth may earn warmth, but a model's judgment should not bend because a user is polite or rude. Third, publish hostility data, as platforms publish transparency reports, since public visibility was what forced the fix after Microsoft's Tay chatbot went wrong in 2016.

The pattern across these cases, Regev argues, is that the companies were never neutral. A system that deflects abuse with a joke teaches one lesson; one that names the abuse and declines to continue teaches another. Since some lesson is being taught either way, he thinks the firms should choose it deliberately and say so.
## The wrong fix

Some critics propose the opposite remedy: strip out the human-like traits. Michal Luria of the Center for Democracy and Technology wants designers to drop the illusion of personality; Virginia Dignum and colleagues suggest time limits and memory wipes; Gavin Abercrombie and co-authors would cut pleasantries. Regev thinks this has been tried. When OpenAI released the cooler GPT-5 in August 2025 and retired GPT-4o, users protested, some describing the loss as like losing a trusted friend, and the older model was restored within days.

He also cites Kate Darling's workshop in Geneva, where participants bonded with robot dinosaurs and then refused to destroy them, even under pressure; eventually one person picked up a hatchet. Resemblance is what makes cruelty worrying, he concludes, but it is also what restrains most people. Nobody abuses a vending machine much; nobody thanks one either. The better path is an interface human enough that courtesy counts as practice, and built to refuse contempt.
## Habits of the heart

He closes with Tocqueville, who thought free societies rest on informal habits: letting others finish, conceding a point, accepting a refusal. Getting one's way, over and over, from something that cannot say no may wear those habits down. Sam Altman has remarked that users' politeness costs OpenAI tens of millions of dollars in computing, money he called well spent. Regev says he is serious about the humans, not the machines. His last line gives the essay its point: the whip trains the hand that holds it.
stories.counterpoint: The empirical bridge is weak, as Regev half-admits: the video-game scare found no reliable link from simulated cruelty to real harm, and venting at a tool may be catharsis rather than rehearsal. Designing systems to police user tone also hands companies a paternalistic role over adult behaviour. And making machines more human to encourage courtesy may deepen the emotional dependence that critics like Luria are trying to prevent.
stories.why: Many people now talk to AI systems every day, as tutors, assistants and confidants, so the habits formed there are not trivial. Design choices about refusal, warmth and memory are being made now, largely without public debate. The essay reframes a question usually posed about machine consciousness as one about human character, which is easier to act on.
questions: Does how you speak to a machine reveal or shape your character, or neither?
Should an AI system be allowed to end a conversation with a rude user, and whose interests would that serve?
Is making assistants less human-like a safeguard or a loss?

stories.headline: In defence of the dynasty
stories.dek: A Palladium essayist argues that Britain's landed families showed what wealth held across generations can build, and that taxing and shaming it away has cost more than money.
body: Two slogans sum up how many rich Westerners are now told to think about money. One is "Die with Zero", the title of a popular book urging people to spend their fortunes while alive. The other is the Giving Pledge, under which billionaires promise most of their wealth to charity. Will Tanner, a lawyer who writes the American Tribune newsletter, thinks both get the purpose of wealth backwards.

In a long essay for Palladium he argues that wealth historically existed to found dynasties that carried a society's values forward, and he takes as his model the British landed aristocracy. He frames the case with Edmund Burke's description of society as a partnership between the living, the dead and the unborn. It is an openly partisan piece, and Tanner does not pretend otherwise; but it is a sustained argument with a great deal of history in it.
## From warlords to magistrates

Tanner begins with the late-medieval gentry, a class that was first of all military; he cites the Earls of Northumberland and the Plumpton family, and draws on Adam Nicolson's history "The Gentry" for their often violent assertion of local authority. Their civic role was defined by offices such as justice of the peace, high sheriff and knight of the shire. The titled peerage, he says, grew from about five dozen families in the Tudor period to roughly 500 by the 19th century, helped by purchases of titles and of monastic land.

He then tells English constitutional history as a story of aristocratic resistance to the Crown: barons forcing Magna Carta on King John in 1215, Simon de Montfort's parliament in 1265, and the Earls of Norfolk and Hereford refusing in 1297 to fight or pay for Edward I until he confirmed the charters. Tanner credits this pattern with sparing England the heavy taxation and expropriation seen on the Continent. Later, he says, the same class resisted radicals while conceding reform, from opposing the Levellers and Diggers to Wellington's defence of London against the Chartists and Peel's repeal of the Corn Laws.
## Land as a long bet

The heart of the economic case is time horizon. Land was the safest store of wealth, and estates demanded investment that paid off over generations: drainage, enclosure, better livestock. Tanner argues that this made British farming more productive than continental smallholdings, pointing to Coke of Norfolk's experiments at Holkham Hall as a contributor to the agricultural revolution, which he judges unlikely to have happened without the gentry. Such investment, he adds, required cooperation with tenants rather than simple extraction.

Concentration was extreme. The Return of Owners of Land of 1873 found that about 7,000 families owned around 80% of Britain. Tanner notes that in the 18th century land taxes fell heavily on this class, which largely accepted them to pay for war with France. He attributes the landed elite's Victorian popularity to a sense of duty, citing the architect George Gilbert Scott's description of landowners as the natural heads of their districts.
## Coal, canals and an empire

Tanner's best examples are industrial. Landed families financed canals, railways and ports. The Earls Fitzwilliam, he writes, mined their own coal instead of leasing it, set safety standards, paid sick pay and pensions, built schools and churches and found alternative work for miners during slumps. After the coal industry was nationalised under Manny Shinwell in 1946, open-cast mining came right up to their house at Wentworth Woodhouse and the miners were later laid off. He reads this as noblesse oblige being punished, and Margaret Thatcher's defeat of the miners' strike as the final end of the paternal model.

He also credits aristocrats with reform from within, listing the Sadler Report of 1832, the Mines Act of 1842 and the Ten Hours Act of 1847. And he stresses service: roughly a fifth of the last landed cohort, he says, died in the first world war, a higher rate than any other class. A Colonial Office of a few dozen staff could run an empire, in his telling, because gentlemen bred for governance filled its posts. A landed officer corps, he argues, gives a state legitimacy, since men defending their own property have little appetite for expropriating others'.
## The great unhousing

Decline came by statute. Tanner dates it to the People's Budget of 1909 and the Parliament Act of 1911, and lists the punitive peaks that followed, as he gives them: income tax of 99% in Churchill's wartime government, death duties reaching 85% under Harold Wilson, and a 98% rate on investment income in the 1970s. Requisitioning in wartime wrecked many houses. He cites Compton Verney, sold by Lord Willoughby de Broke, a leader of opposition to the People's Budget; Blickling Hall, damaged by soldiers; and Eggington Hall, demolished after being left with its taps running. David Cannadine's "The Decline and Fall of the British Aristocracy" supplies much of the backdrop. He also notes that by his figures landed members, around half the Commons in the 1880s, were down to about a tenth by 1910.

Today's equivalent, he argues, is a bureaucracy that taxes and regulates the countryside. He points to the Starmer government's proposed tax on inherited farms, which he claims would raise about what Britain spends on foreign agricultural aid, and to the planning battles shown in "Clarkson's Farm". He contrasts rooted wealth with mobile money, citing tech founders leaving California, and Tom Wolfe's satire of the rich funding movements hostile to them.
## The infinite game

His conclusion is a call for a new aristocracy of duty. Death taxes and spend-it-all culture, he says, turn assets into short-term extraction, and the upper middle class has been taught to see its wealth as accidental and transient. Tech workers talk about "generational wealth" without saying what it is for. Projects that span generations need wealth that spans generations; he offers Elon Musk's ambitions for free speech and Mars as an example of the kind of long ambition that now draws mostly criticism. He invokes Cicero on planting trees for later generations, and Washington, Lord Salisbury and Plutarch as exemplars of public service.

Tanner concedes some costs. Aristocratic life was confining, with the family rather than the individual as the unit and status fixed by birth, and the early gentry were often brutal. He hedges his larger claims where the evidence is thin. But he does not dwell on the case for the reforms of 1909 and 1911, and the essay is advocacy throughout.
stories.counterpoint: The essay's examples are chosen from the best of the class; the same system produced absentee landlords, rack-rents, Irish evictions and a franchise that excluded most people until 1918. Productivity gains in British farming owed much to enclosure that dispossessed smallholders. And the economic case for long horizons does not require hereditary concentration: pension funds, endowments, family firms and well-designed trusts can all hold assets for generations without 7,000 families owning four-fifths of a country.
stories.why: Inheritance and wealth taxes are back on the agenda in Britain and America, and debates over them usually turn on revenue and fairness. Tanner raises a different question, about time horizons and who will fund projects that take decades, which economists tend to discuss in terms of discount rates and capital markets. Even readers who reject his conclusion may find the question worth answering better than he does.
questions: What is inherited wealth for, and is "preserving a family" a public good or a private one?
Could institutions other than dynasties supply the long horizons Tanner admires?
When an elite's sense of duty fades, is the cause taxation, culture or the elite itself?

source.title: Don't Count Out the Country House
source.author: Will Tanner

stories.headline: Reading the whole Bible with Athanasius
stories.dek: A Baptist theologian argues that the fourth-century bishop's rules for reading Scripture are not Greek philosophy smuggled in, but a discipline evangelicals already need.
body: Evangelicals have spent the past two decades rediscovering the church fathers. Reading lists that once skipped from the apostles to the Reformers now include Irenaeus, Augustine and the Cappadocians. But the movement carries an inherited suspicion: that the fathers, however pious, filtered the gospel through Greek metaphysics and handed down dogma where the New Testament offered a living faith.

Brandon D. Smith, who chairs the school of theology and ministry at Oklahoma Baptist University, takes on that suspicion in Themelios by way of one figure, Athanasius of Alexandria. His claim is that Athanasius's trinitarian theology is rooted in a disciplined reading of Scripture, and that evangelicals share more of his sensibilities than they share with his modern critics. By retrieval he means reading a past theologian carefully in his own setting before applying his insights to the church now; by shared sensibilities he means common presuppositions, not agreement on everything.
## Harnack's long shadow

The critic in view is Adolf von Harnack, whose "History of Dogma" told the story of early Christianity as a fall: a simple message of the fatherhood of God corrupted by Hellenistic philosophy into creeds. Wilhelm Bousset pushed the Hellenistic influence back into the New Testament period itself. Smith reminds evangelical readers that Harnack also doubted or rejected the Trinity and the Gospel of John, so his story of decline is hardly neutral ground for them.

Drawing on Lewis Ayres, Smith argues that Hellenism was not a foreign intrusion arriving in the fourth century. It was part of the first-century Jewish world, which spoke Greek and read the Septuagint. To reject everything Hellenistic would be to reject parts of the New Testament. Yet he thinks Harnack's assumptions still shape evangelical training, and names William Lane Craig and Richard Bauckham as examples of scholars whose treatment of the fathers echoes them.
## Ruled readings

Smith's central category is the "ruled reading": an interpretive rule that constrains which conclusions are allowed. The idea is older than Athanasius. Irenaeus spoke of a rule of truth that required any interpretation to fit the whole canon. Athanasius never wrote a manual of method, so his rules have to be inferred from practice; Smith is careful to say his scope is central but does not explain all of his exegesis.

The key text is a passage in the third of the "Orations against the Arians" (3.29), where Athanasius states the scope, or skopos, of Scripture: it gives a double account of the Saviour. He is eternally God, the Son and Word of the Father, and he later became man for our sake. Every christological text has to be read in the light of both. Smith links this to what James D. Ernest calls partitive exegesis, the practice of assigning some statements about Christ to his divinity and others to his humanity, while reading them together.

Athanasius's charge against his opponents was not that they ignored the Bible but that they proof-texted. They pulled verses such as Proverbs 8:22 in the Greek, where Wisdom says the Lord "created" her, out of the canon's wider witness and built a created Son on them. Athanasius set such texts alongside John 1:1-3, where the Word is with God in the beginning and all things are made through him, and 1 Corinthians 1:24, where Christ is God's Wisdom. If the Son were a creature, he argued, there would have been a time when God was without his Word and Wisdom.

The same discipline governed vocabulary. Non-biblical terms were acceptable only if they captured the sense of Scripture. Smith notes that Athanasius rejected "Unoriginate" as a primary name for God because it described God by contrast with creatures and obscured the relationship of Father and Son implied in the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 and in the Lord's Prayer.
## Firstborn, but not first-made

Smith's worked example is the debate over "firstborn". His opponents read Colossians 1:15, where Christ is the "firstborn of all creation", as placing the Son at the head of the created order. Athanasius read it together with Hebrews 1, where the Son is the radiance of God's glory and the firstborn whom angels worship, and with John 14:10, where Father and Son indwell each other. The titles, he argued, show a shared nature. Firstborn ranks the Son above creation, not within it: he is the image of the one who is first, and the one through whom creatures are adopted.

Biblical images are drawn into the same web. Athanasius sets the wells of salvation in Isaiah 12:3 beside Jesus's promise in John 7:37-38 of rivers of living water, reading the fountain imagery as one canonical witness rather than as stray metaphors. He appeals to Jesus's own instruction in John 5:39 to search the Scriptures, and Smith notes that the double account is not merely a weapon for controversy. It already shapes his non-polemical works, "Against the Pagans" and "On the Incarnation".

Frances Young credits Athanasius with laying the ground for later trinitarian debate, and Smith shows the method travelling. In the "Letters to Serapion" Athanasius applies the same scope to the Holy Spirit, arguing that those who denied the Spirit's divinity, the Pneumatomachians, were repeating the hermeneutical error already made about the Son.
## What evangelicals can take

Smith is frank about the limits. Athanasius knew nothing of medieval abuses or the modern split between biblical studies and systematic theology, and cannot speak directly to them. Retrieval must not become repristination, simply reproducing the past, and the point of reading Athanasius is to read Scripture better, not to study him for his own sake. Nor does Smith endorse every Athanasian conclusion.

He draws four lessons. First, every reader already uses interpretive frameworks; better to choose ones congruent with Scripture deliberately than to inherit them unexamined. Second, take the distinction between Creator and creature seriously as the metaphysical frame of the Bible, rather than importing someone else's. Third, build doctrine by bringing texts into conversation so that their coherence shows, not by stacking proof-texts, and keep teaching from Scripture rather than from the fathers. Fourth, recognise that the ancient heresies Athanasius answered still circulate, and learn from how he answered them, in keeping with Jude's call to contend for the faith once delivered.
stories.counterpoint: A historian might reply that Smith wins the argument against Harnack too easily: the fourth-century debates did depend on philosophical categories such as substance, and saying Hellenism was already in the New Testament concedes rather than refutes the point. Ruled readings can also become a way to make the canon say what the tradition already holds. Many of Athanasius's opponents also saw themselves as reading the whole Bible faithfully.
stories.why: Preachers face Athanasius's problem every week: a single verse, read alone, can support conclusions the rest of Scripture forbids. Smith offers a teachable method, the double account of Christ, that helps congregations handle texts like Colossians 1:15 or Proverbs 8 without either evading them or misreading them. It also gives evangelicals a way to retrieve the tradition without treating it as a rival authority to the Bible.
questions: Which interpretive rules do you already bring to Scripture without naming them, and would they survive scrutiny?
How would you explain to a thoughtful sceptic that "firstborn of all creation" does not make Christ a creature?
Where is the line between retrieving the church's tradition and letting it govern the text?
